Surgical curettage may promote dissemination of the parasite.36 Other local treatments include cryotherapy or, alternative- ly, application of heat to bring the temperature of the lesion to about 40° which may aid healing.37 Topical treatment with paromomycin sulfate 15% plus methylbenzethonium chloride 5 or 12% has produced promising responses;38-41 paromomycin 12 to 15% with urea 10% was better tolerat- ed.42 However, not all studies have shown benefit.43,44 Systemic treatment is similar to that of visceral leishmaniasis3,5,45,46 (see above). Topical paromomycin plus systemic meglumine antimonate was initially found to be promising in patients with New World infections,47 but a subsequent randomised, controlled study48 found that application of paromomycin sulfate 15% with methyl- benzethonium chloride 12% did not augment the clinical response to parenteral meglumine antimonate. Cutaneous leishmaniasis due to L. aethiopica, including diffuse cuta- neous leishmaniasis, does not generally respond to antimonials3 although responses to antimonials with paro- momycin have been reported.49 It may also be treated with pentamidine.3,5 Other drugs tried in cutaneous leishmaniasis have included fluconazole,50 itraconazole,51-54 and ketoconazole.41,55-58 Variable responses to allopurinol have been reported in pa- tients with New World infections.59-61 Dapsone was re- ported to be effective in a study in patients in India62 but not in Colombia.63 Among the non-specific therapies tried in cutaneous leishmaniasis, topical application of the nitric oxide donor S-nitroso-N-acetylpenicillamine (SNAP)64 and intralesional injection of hypertonic sodium chloride solution65 have produced beneficial responses. Immu- nomodulation using leishmania antigens mixed with BCG,66,67 or interferon gamma,68,69 has produced encour- aging results. While there has been some work on vaccines against cuta- neous leishmaniasis much more needs to be done. Howev- er, leishmanisation (deliberate infection with L. major) has been used as a last resort in some countries when other measures have failed. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis of the New World (espun- dia) is caused by L. braziliensis or L. panamensis. In mu- cocutaneous leishmaniasis the primary lesions do not heal spontaneously. Metastatic spread to the mucosa may occur during the presence of the primary lesion or up to 30 years later. The nasal mucosa is always affected.
